Inductive charging may also reduce the minimum required battery storage (and thus costs) needed to be installed on each vehicle by regularly replenishing the state of charge of a comparatively smaller battery to maintain desired operations. Further, the capital, operating, and maintenance costs of the charging infrastructure will be a major engineering and financial factor. For example, the capital cost of the 16-position Level 3 DC fast-charging station shown in Figure 25 is estimated to be $2.5 million, not including additional cost for any changes to the electrical grid necessary to ensure sufficient primary power supply voltage and amperage at the selected charging facility location. 4.4 Station/Curbfront Configurations and Associated Infrastructure Fundamental to future AMDs is the prospect of AV fleets providing public mobility services using the common public roadway network and associated common infrastructure, independent of whether the fleets are owned and operated by a transit authority, contracted to an operator, or offered by a private company providing ride-hailing services—or some combination thereof. Similarly, whether public or private, all types of PUDO locations can be referred to as “stations” and “station facilities” whether they comprise the curbfront at the side of a road (as in the case of PUDO zones) or a more substantive form of boarding and alighting infrastructure reminiscent of more traditional transit stations. The state of the art for ODT services (whether automated or manually controlled) is to have predefined locations where the passenger can meet the vehicle near their physical original location. Figure 26 shows the roadway network and programmed points on the network where passengers can access the RAPID service at Arlington, Texas. Such locations are dense enough to minimize the walking distance to the rendezvous point where the dispatched vehicle will meet the passenger—typically about one block away, yet predetermined to ensure there is adequate curb space for safe vehicle access. 47 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Source: City of Arlington Provision for safe and efficient pickup and drop-off (PUDO) station locations for automated operations away from the roadway network’s main travel lanes requires additional or rededicated space, the specifications of which will scale with demand. This additional area could be as simple and inexpensive as the reuse of existing curb space or a dedicated lane (perhaps replacing some on-street parking) for low-demand, occasional PUDO operations. As passenger demand at a location increases, a station may require dedicated space completely off the roadway right-of- way—such as within the first level of a parking garage near the roadway.
